content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its guidelines to improve access to healthcare workers in remote and rural areas by enhancing their retention. These guidelines, originally published in 2010, focus on strategies to attract, recruit, and retain health workers in underserved regions. The recommendations are evidence-based and aim to address the internal movement of health workers within countries, ensuring their availability in rural and remote areas. The guidelines emphasize the importance of scaling up and transforming health professional education and training. They advocate for producing graduates who are responsive to the health needs of the populations they serve. Educational institutions are encouraged to implement institutional and instructional reforms and to foster collaboration between education, health, and other sectors. These reforms are closely tied to the retention of health workers in rural areas. The WHO Global Code of Practice on the International Recruitment of Health Personnel, adopted in 2010, addresses international health worker mobility and the strengthening of health systems. It encourages member states to adopt measures to address the geographical maldistribution of health workers and to support their retention in underserved areas. The Code promotes international solidarity and equity in health workforce-related matters, aligning with the goals of the rural retention guidelines. The guidelines also explore the role of targeted admission policies, such as enrolling students with rural backgrounds in health education programs, to increase the likelihood of these graduates practicing in rural areas. Additionally, they examine the impact of exposing undergraduate students to rural community experiences and clinical rotations, as well as incorporating rural health topics into curricula, on improving rural retention. Continuing education and professional development programs tailored to the needs of rural health workers, accessible where they live and work, are highlighted as critical for retention. The introduction of enhanced scopes of practice for rural health workers and the deployment of different types of health workers with appropriate training and regulation are also recommended strategies. The guidelines stress the importance of providing a supportive working environment, including adequate equipment, supplies, supervision, and mentoring, to improve retention. Financial incentives, such as hardship allowances, housing grants, free transportation, and paid vacations, are identified as effective tools for retaining rural health workers. Improved living conditions, infrastructure, and services for health workers and their families in rural areas are also emphasized. The use of telehealth and outreach activities to facilitate collaboration between health workers in better-served and underserved areas is recommended to enhance rural retention. Career development programs and the provision of senior posts in rural areas are also suggested as strategies to improve retention. The guidelines are part of WHO's broader efforts to optimize community health worker programs, improve health labor market analysis, and address workplace violence in the health sector. They aim to provide national governments and partners with the tools to design, implement, and evaluate effective health workforce policies, contributing to the realization of universal health coverage.
